question_en:
Nav2 Custom Costmap plugin subscription [closed]

Closed 5 days ago.

I am trying to write a costmap plugin for nav2 and i need to get a specific data from a topic but i couldnt create and spin the subscription inside the plugin. (I need coordinate points to create an obstacle at those points)
evidence: The question asks how to create and spin a ROS 2 subscription inside a custom Nav2 costmap layer plugin, for example by getting the node from the plugin's node handle and calling create_subscription in onInitialize. None of the remaining passages give this. They are navigation menus, plugin lists, and tutorial section titles such as 'Write a new Costmap2D plugin' with no content. Passage 6 only says the static layer subscribes to an OccupancyGrid topic and that developers may write their own layers, without saying how to set up a subscription in plugin code.

question_en:
I am procedurally generating planets for an open world space sandbox game. I am using a rough simulation of tectonic plates to create mountain ranges and other geological features.

A planet surface consists of several plates, which consists of tiles. The continental plates are randomly generated, w
evidence: Passage 14 is enough on its own to answer the question. It says oceanic crust moves away from mid-ocean ridges, the divergent spreading sites, and eventually meets continental crust. That meeting happens either at active margins, which are real plate boundaries, or at passive margins. Passive margins 'are not plate boundaries, but areas where a single tectonic plate transitions from oceanic lithosphere to continental lithosphere.' Its example is Mid-Atlantic Ridge crust becoming part of the passive margin on the North American or Eurasian plate. So the land–ocean transition on the flank of a divergent boundary occurs within one plate rather than at the boundary itself. This addresses why the asker finds no 'land-ocean divergent boundary' and implies that plates are not purely 'land' or 'ocean'. Passages 8 (East African Rift as a continental divergent boundary that may come to behave like a mid-ocean ridge) and 10 (Mid-Atlantic Ridge separating plates) add support but do not cover the land-ocean case on their own.

question_en: This is more of a terminological question, but I think it fits here. I've been reading a book by Rachel Carson, from the early 50s, and she uses the phrase "Archaeozic period". I haven't seen this used elsewhere - is it just an archaic (pardon the pun) form of "Archean", or does it describe a differ
evidence: The question asks whether Carson's 'Archaeozoic' is an older name for the Archean or a different period. None of the passages mention the term 'Archaeozoic' or discuss historical geologic time nomenclature. Passage 16 mentions the Eoarchean Era and the Hadean Eon, and passages 11, 12 and 18 list ice ages by period, but none of them explain the relationship between Archaeozoic and Archean. An answer would have to rely entirely on general knowledge.

question_en: I am trying to understand the concrete process of how a meteorologist at a weather forecast office produces the different types of weather forecasts. I understand how numerical weather models work, but I would like to learn how the model output is turned into a forecast and to what extend it is impr
evidence: The question asks how forecasters at a weather forecast office turn numerical model output into forecasts: which model outputs they look at, and how much they rely on local observations and experience. None of the passages describe that workflow. Passages 5, 6, 11 and 12 (Hong Kong 9-day forecast) cover only product definitions and accuracy statistics. Passages 3, 9, 10 and 13–19 cover the OVATION aurora model, which is space weather. Passages 2 and 4 are about how seasons are defined, and the rest (economics nowcasting, psychology, magnets and plants, an NSSL navigation menu) are unrelated. At most an assistant could offer loosely related facts, not an answer to what was asked.

question_en:
Can a bacterium infect another bacterium?
I researched about it by searching on Google and reading some bacteriological articles, but I did not get any answer. I also asked some of my teachers, and they were also a bit confused. Some said that it is possible and others said not. So the question rema
evidence: The passages cover infection in general: pathogen types, human hosts, colonization, diagnosis and treatment. They also mention bacterial endosymbionts of insects and bacterial genomes. None describes a bacterium infecting, parasitizing or living inside another bacterium (e.g., Bdellovibrio or bacteria-within-bacteria endosymbiosis), so the question cannot be answered.

question_en:
People who climb the social hierarchy

We know that people on top of the social hierarchy have (at least in developed countries) 30 or more years average life expectancy , more stable marriages, happier life and so on. So my question is for people who managed to get from the bottom to the top, what
evidence: The question asks whether people who move from the bottom to the top of the social hierarchy end up with outcomes (divorce rate, life expectancy, happiness) more like the bottom or the top. None of the passages addresses this. The PMC5494206 review only says in general that status affects health and wellness. The economic-inequality passage covers country-level inequality and life expectancy, not individual upward mobility. The other passages are off-topic.

question_en:
Why use a quasi experimental design when you can do an experiment?

I read about quasi-experimental design and the variations it has such as pre-test post-test non-equivalent groups, and also experimental designs. Having compared these two, I ascertained that the difference between this variation of
evidence: The question asks why quasi-experiments exist if randomization is easy. Four passages each answer this on their own by explaining when randomization is not feasible or not ethical. Passage 0 gives a depression-therapy example: doctors consider random assignment unethical, so researchers use pre-existing groups instead. Passage 2 says quasi-experimental designs are useful when randomization is not possible or ethical, or when a true experiment is too expensive; they can use data already collected (often by the government), and they have higher external validity. Passage 7 says quasi-experiments are conducted in field settings where random assignment is difficult or impossible, for example when evaluating psychotherapy or educational interventions. Passage 1 describes natural experiments (the Oregon Medicaid lottery) and regression discontinuity, where assignment is set by outside events or by cutoffs rather than by the researcher. Passage 8 only notes that students are not randomly assigned to classes, which is weaker. Passage 3 says these designs are implemented more often than randomized ones, and that regression discontinuity lets the program be assigned to those who need or deserve it most; this is a reason, but more partial.

question_en:
How can humans tell when something diverges from the norm

With this I mean the notion of humans being able to, for example, look at a painting and tell that something doesn't belong in there. For example sun glasses on the Mona Lisa, without prior knowledge of the painting. I just find it easier to
evidence: The question asks how humans detect that something in a scene does not belong, such as sunglasses on the Mona Lisa. That would need material on scene schemas, expectation violation, or semantic incongruity detection, and none of the passages covers this. Passage 11 explains Gestalt grouping principles for illusions, but not anomaly detection, and the asker already found Gestalt unhelpful. Passage 28 covers the cortex anticipating sensory input from the body's own eye movements, not spotting out-of-place objects. Passage 3 says neural networks need training data to recognize things, which is only loosely related. The remaining passages are fiction, reference lists, or unrelated topics.

question_en:
I'm trying to solve the following problem. The sea level in the past was 200 m higher than today. The seawater became in isostatic equilibrium with the ocean basin. what is the increase in the depth x
 of the ocean basins? Water density is ρw=1000 kg m−3
, and mantle density is 3300 kg m−3
.

U
evidence: The question asks why the user's isostatic compensation-column calculation for ocean-basin deepening is wrong. Answering it needs the isostatic balance principle: the extra water column must include the depression x itself, so ρw(200+x) = ρm·x. None of the passages state this principle or any compensation-column formula. Post-glacial rebound passages describe isostatic depression and rebound only qualitatively. The vertical pressure variation passages give hydrostatic pressure (ρgh) but say nothing about isostatic equilibrium. The sea and ocean passages give sea-level history and seawater properties. Correcting the derivation would have to come from general knowledge, not the knowledge base.

question_en:
What are some negative/positive aspects from globalization in regard to developed countries?

I have read many articles on how globalization is helping developing countries, as more and more companies from developed countries have been moving their production oversees. However, as hard as I tried, I
evidence: Passage 1 (National Geographic, effects of economic globalization) speaks directly to effects relevant to developed economies. On the positive side, businesses gain a competitive advantage by sourcing cheap raw materials and lower-cost labor while still leveraging the technical expertise of developed economies. Consumers benefit from lower prices and a wider variety of goods, though this is linked to both healthier diets and more unhealthy food consumption. On the negative side, communities that depended on outsourced jobs suffer, and workers in the developed world must compete with lower-cost markets. Unions may be unable to resist corporations that offer a choice between lower pay and losing jobs to cheaper markets. This goes beyond unemployment/GDP to cover consumer prices, variety, health effects, and worker bargaining power. Passage 10 adds income inequality and wage pressure on unskilled workers, but it is not framed specifically around developed countries. The Brexit passages (19-21) discuss the benefits of trade and FDI for the UK, but only loosely in the context of Brexit.

So i was making a electron project that records your screen and your desktop or selected app's audio with desktopCapture. I got the screen record, and at one point even got the mic to work, but at no point, no matter what i tried, i couldn'

question_en:
How to use sea water in daily life?

Here in my place there is a shortage of river water during these days because of lack of rain. People are demanding to use sea water where we can so please suggest the ways in which we can use sea water...
evidence: Passage 10 (wiki/water-resources.md) gives a direct, on-topic answer for a water shortage. It explains that seawater can be turned into fresh water by desalination, mainly through distillation or reverse osmosis. It also says this is costly but can be economically practical for household uses in arid or water-short areas. Passage 16 adds that untreated seawater is too salty to drink, but on its own that is only a caution, not a way to use seawater. The other sea passages (aquaculture, leisure, the sea as a heat sink for power stations, seawater pumped storage) do not address everyday household substitutes for river water.

I am following the paper to calculate UTCI using ERA5 meteorological variables.

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00484-020-01900-5?shared-article-renderer

In the paper, the authors have mentioned that they are using ERA5 product. And specifically mentioned to use the direct and diffu
evidence: None of the remaining passages explain how to get direct and diffuse surface shortwave from ERA5. That would mean naming ERA5's direct-radiation variable, or describing a decomposition method that gives diffuse as total minus direct. Passage 0 is only a general ERA5 overview listing levels and resolution, and passage 10 is an empty Climate Data Store page. The gmd passages mention solar direct radiation at the top of the atmosphere for contrail radiative forcing, which is unrelated to splitting surface shortwave for UTCI.

question_en:
What will be the Effect of the Russian oil Price Cap

G7 countries have just announced that they will not buy oil from Russia unless the price is USD 60/barrel or below. What will be the effect of this cap- will it be an effective economic sanction? Why can’t Russia sell the oil to a non G7 intermed
evidence: Passage 1 explains the price cap's mechanism and intended effects. It aims to curtail Russian profits while keeping oil supply stable by keeping Russian exports on the market, avoiding a price spike. It works by requiring any sale involving coalition-based companies, such as insurers or flagging companies, to be at or below the cap. This bears on why an intermediary cannot simply resell the oil. It also notes that sanctions are enforced against vessels carrying oil priced above the cap. Passage 2 describes the actual effect: the EU embargo and the price cap forced sizeable discounts on Russian exporters, and Russian energy revenues fell by almost 40% (Jan–Oct 2023 vs 2022). The targeted sanctions avoided the supply shock markets had feared, and global oil prices declined. Enforcement of the cap continues to limit revenues, putting pressure on Russia's budget. Passage 0 (footnote iii) adds supporting detail on the maritime-services restriction but on its own does not address effectiveness or the market price.

question_en:
What is the scientific term for the tendency to see familiar patterns in things, that are actually something completely different?

What is the scientific term for the tendency to see familiar patterns in things, that are actually something completely different? One of the most common examples of th
evidence: The term the user wants is pareidolia. Passage 15, in the 'Cognitive illusions' section of the optical illusion article, has an image caption reading "'The Organ Player' – Pareidolia phenomenon in Neptune's Grotto stalactite cave". It names pareidolia as the phenomenon of seeing a familiar figure (an organ player) in an unrelated formation (stalactites), and files it under cognitive illusions. An assistant can therefore name the term using general knowledge only to interpret it. Passage 13 (Gestalt: the brain has a need to see familiar simple objects) is related but does not name the term.

question_en:
Can you accelerate the growth of a plant by accelerating its surroundings?
I had this weird idea of making plants grow faster when I first visited an indoor nursery which used floodlights instead of sunlight. They turned on during the day and went off during night in cycles.
If the time period of th
evidence: The question asks whether shortening artificial light/dark cycles (faster day-night cycles) would make plants grow faster or let later generations adapt; this concerns circadian rhythms and photoperiod. Every remaining passage comes from a forum thread about growing plants with magnets: magnetized water, magnetized seeds and magnetic fields affecting O2 output. None covers light-cycle length, photoperiod, circadian clocks or multi-generational adaptation, so no passage supports an on-topic answer.

Is Polyacrylamide a material used to make microbeads?

evidence: No passage mentions polyacrylamide or says whether it is used to make microbeads. Passage 1 only says that microplastic abrasive beads (under 5 mm) are used in some toothpastes and harm the environment, without naming the polymers involved. I am trying to delete some entries based on 'name'. I have a table t1 with different columns, one of them being name and of type NCLOB. I have a method to delete these entries in Java, and I am using a named query
evidence: The question asks how to fix ORA-00932 (inconsistent datatypes) when comparing an Oracle NCLOB column with = in a DELETE, for example by using DBMS_LOB.COMPARE or TO_CHAR. None of the remaining passages covers Oracle LOB comparison or that error. The Oracle passages are only site navigation and footer links. So why are most of the craters radially symmetric?

Why isn't the depression
evidence: The question asks why impact craters are circular even though most impacts are oblique. None of the passages explains this. Where can I find a calculator for constrained optimization of general form of algebraic equation?

I'm working with a fairly complex equation and I need to carry out constrained optimization of the same. The first order differential equations are very messy to solve by hand and hence I thought to us
evidence: The question asks for a symbolic constrained-optimization tool (an online calculator or software such as Matlab) that can keep parameters like a and b symbolic. Passages 10 and 11 are only navigation menus listing generic calculators (equation, derivative, etc.), with nothing about symbolic constrained optimization. question_en:
Set interface name without msg in ROS2

When creating custom message types in ROS1 (noetic), I can store the *.msg files in a subfolder named msg. In the CMake file, I just type the name of the file without msg/ in add_message_files(...). The resulting message type is named as <pkg_name>/<file-name
evidence: The question asks whether the generated ROS 2 interface name can be decoupled from the msg/ folder path used in rosidl_generate_interfaces. No passage covers rosidl_generate_interfaces, interface naming conventions, or whether the msg namespace can be changed. The custom-interfaces tutorials appear only as navigation links (10, 12, 13). Passage 4 only notes that ROS 1 packages keep message types in a msg/ folder, and passage 1 only shows the gz.msgs naming used by Gazebo. Neither addresses the question.

question_en:
Identify kind of descriptive role playing game for self-discovery

There's a comic book called "Knights of the Dinner Table" about a bunch of rpg players.

In one issue, the only girl at the table GM's some kind of self-discovery game she learnt in her psychology class. She describes some situations
evidence: The question asks for the name of the real psychology self-discovery exercise (a guided imagery or symbolic journey, often called 'The Cube' or a similar personality game) that the Knights of the Dinner Table story is based on. None of the passages identify such an exercise. Passage 8 covers psychological assessment by a psychological doctor, the RPG blog passages are navigation boilerplate, and the book excerpts are unrelated fiction (the dancing bears in passage 0 are a coincidence).

question_en:
Opposite of White Bear principle?

Is there any phrase/term to describe the opposite of White Bear principle (also known as ironic process principle)? I'm looking for a word to describe the process where something eludes you the more you try to think of it (or remember it). I think I may have come a
evidence: Passage 6 describes the 'tip of the tongue' phenomenon: a state where a familiar word cannot be retrieved despite a feeling of imminent retrieval. It was first described by William James, Freud linked it to forgetting familiar words, and Brown & McNeill studied it empirically. This fits the user's description of something eluding you when you try to remember it. Passage 16 explicitly mentions 'ironic effects of attempting to remember', i.e. memory attempts that paradoxically fail depending on mental control, which also names the phenomenon the user describes.

question_en: What is the scientific reason for the majestic sights of the northern and southern lights, otherwise known as Auroras near the magnetic poles, and why do the northern lights differ from the southern lights?
evidence: The passages can answer the first part of the question (what causes the aurora), but none explains why the northern lights differ from the southern lights. On the cause: passage 11 says discrete aurorae come from accelerated particles (quasi-static electric fields, Alfvén waves). It says diffuse aurorae come from equatorial magnetosphere plasma sheet particles scattered into the loss cone by chorus waves. Passage 12 says the visible colors come from collisions and chemical reactions: green and red light from atomic oxygen, and violet/blue and deep-red light from nitrogen. Passage 0 links the aurora to electron and proton precipitation driven by the solar wind and the interplanetary magnetic field. On the north–south difference: passage 12 only notes that the study focuses on the northern hemisphere because the aurora is more accessible for viewing there.

question_en:
CO2 emissions from outdoor fire pit

I have an outdoor fire pit in my backyard. The fire pit is about 3 feet in diameter and is similar to ones you might find at a camp site. My family and I enjoy using it purely for recreation. I’ve been trying to limit my carbon footprint, and in doing so, wondere
evidence: None of the passages gives an emission figure for burning wood. There is no CO2 per log, per kilogram of wood or per hour of a campfire, so the main question (pounds of CO2 per hour) cannot be estimated. The passages only say generally that combustion releases CO2 (whatbiocharandhowitmade) and that fire smoke is linked to respiratory illness. The biochar passage gives 3.6 tons of CO2 per ton of biochar, but that refers to biomass left to degrade naturally, not to burning wood. Passing mentions of tar smoke and soot aerosols do not substantively answer the question about other harmful gases from a fire pit.

question_en:
How to publish pose of the lidar/camera/(or any dynamic/static model) in gazebo fortress?

I am trying publish the pose of the camera and view it in rviz2. I am using ros2 Humble and gazebo fortress. I can see the image using the image topic but i am not able to visualize the topic in the gazebo as
evidence: The question asks how to publish a camera/lidar/model pose in Gazebo Fortress (e.g., with the PosePublisher system, including where the plugin must be placed and its parameters) and how to bridge it to ROS 2 so it can be viewed in RViz2. None of the passages covers the PosePublisher system, pose topics, ros_gz bridging of poses/TF, or RViz visualization of poses. Passages 0–8 only describe URDF-to-SDFormat conversion; passages 9–11 and 19 are general Gazebo tutorial slides (CLI, sensors, ECS, plugin interfaces); the rest are navigation indexes or an old ROS camera plugin.

question_en:
Why the eco-friendly soy ink is not abundent on the market?

From time to time I see on different papers "Printed with eco-friendly ink," so I assume that it is the soy-based ink. I have read a bit about it, and the opinions about soy-ink being eco-friendly are split, but I would say that it's defin
evidence: Passage 1 answers the label question and the 'is it just marketing' question. It describes the American Soybean Association's SoySeal, a licensed label with minimum soybean oil content standards per ink type, such as 40% for black news ink. It also says about one-third of US newspaper printers and over 90% of daily newspapers use soy color ink, which shows commercial printers use it widely. Passage 0 gives a partial reason for limited availability: soy ink is slower to dry than many inks. It also explains that soy ink was developed for and adopted by the newspaper industry, which points to commercial printing rather than consumer printers. Neither passage directly explains why consumer printer soy ink is hard to buy.

question_en:
What determines a robots euler rotation order?

I know Fanuc robots use the XYZ rotation order, ABB uses ZYX and some robots use the ZYZ rotation order. What actually determines this order? is it the way the frames are setup on the DH table? Or is it just the order they chose to solve the IK, and an
evidence: The remaining passages come from a Fanuc forum thread about how Fanuc's W,P,R angles work. They say the rotations are extrinsic about the fixed X,Y,Z axes, which is equivalent to intrinsic Z,Y',X'' (yaw-pitch-roll). One poster notes it is hard to find out what standard each manufacturer uses. The rviz code shows several Euler conventions (XYZ, ZYX, ZXZ). None of the passages says what determines a robot's rotation order: whether it is tied to the DH frame setup or the IK solution, or is simply a convention the manufacturer chose. So the core question cannot be answered from these passages.

question_en:
Why isn't economic growth defined in terms of the increase in national wealth?

Economic growth is defined as the increase in production or output per unit time. Why isn't it instead defined in terms of the increase in national wealth?
evidence: The question asks why growth is measured as an increase in output rather than an increase in the stock of national wealth. Passage 0 gives a rationale: mercantilism tied a nation's wealth to its stock of gold, silver and goods, while Adam Smith argued that overall labor and production were the better measure of national wealth. Passage 11 adds that this idea of measuring wealth by production (growing the whole pie rather than holding the largest slice) provided the theoretical foundation for GDP as the measure of a nation's economic health. This is a partial, historical explanation rather than a full conceptual one (e.g., stock vs. flow), but it is on-topic and substantive.
